## Abstract

This article establishes a rigorous theoretical and econometric framework for the development of statistical arbitrage trading strategies. The analysis begins by challenging the classical assumption of normality in financial returns, documenting robust \"stylized facts\" such as leptokurtosis (fat tails), volatility clustering, and the leverage effect. These empirical irregularities necessitate a move beyond simple linear models.

Consequently, the research advances into modeling conditional variance, examining the stationarity of ARMA processes and employing the ARCH/GARCH family of models to capture time-varying risk and volatility persistence. This univariate foundation sets the stage for multivariate analysis.

Finally, the paper addresses the critical distinction between short-term correlation and long-run equilibrium. By contrasting Vector Autoregression (VAR) with Vector Error Correction Models (VECM), we demonstrate why VECM is the superior framework for pairs trading. Through the application of Unit Root (ADF) and Cointegration (Johansen) tests, this study provides the mathematical tools to identify mean-reverting spreads, thereby transforming econometric theory into actionable trading signals.
